Higher-order Cauchy problems: roots, jets and propagation

Original programme exposition and all twenty-three original solved exercises are retained and completed here. Current source and proof review: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, 5 October 2026. This independently written lesson is dedicated under CC0. Linked prerequisite components retain their respective licences, including the separately supplied GFDL 1.2 notices. Approved purchased sources are valid mathematical sources and ordinary citations; no citation replaces a programme proof.

Begin with the scalar first-order Cauchy lesson. Its weak energy and existence theorem supplies each branch evolution below.

The aim is to solve a scalar equation of order mmm by following its mmm simple characteristic branches. The branches separate the equation into first-order evolutions; the initial data remain a vector of normal derivatives. Interpolation reconnects these two descriptions and explains the different Sobolev orders of the data. We then pass from a global symbol model to local differential operators, prove semiglobal existence, and identify the singularities arriving at a noncharacteristic initial surface.

Throughout,

Dt=−i∂t,Dx=−i∂x,(u,v)=∫uv‾, D_t=-i\partial_t,\qquad D_x=-i\partial_x, \qquad (u,v)=\int u\overline v, Dt​=−i∂t​,Dx​=−i∂x​,(u,v)=∫uv,

so the pairing is linear in its first entry. Initial data in this convention are Dtju(0)D_t^ju(0)Dtj​u(0), rather than ∂tju(0)\partial_t^ju(0)∂tj​u(0). The scalar first-order energy and existence theorem is the input from the preceding lesson. The exact earlier programme proofs are ordinary products, adjoints and remainders, all-real global Sobolev maps, actual asymptotic sums and ordered conic parametrices. The proof map identifies the unique used locators and complete earlier closure. Section 4 develops the mixed half-space spaces, duality, one-sided extension and differential normal recovery using exact preceding programme proofs. The boundary calculus retains its distinct supported and restricted distribution meanings.

4. Green's formula, existence and the missing trace step

Mixed spaces, restrictions and the one-sided multipliers

Before constructing a weak solution, establish the normal regularity and trace tools that will identify its Cauchy jets. Write

h(ξ)=⟨ξ⟩,R(τ,ξ)=⟨(τ,ξ)⟩,∥U∥(r,q)2=(2π)−(n+1)∫R2rh2q∣U^(τ,ξ)∣2 dτ dξ.(HC37) h(\xi)=\langle\xi\rangle,\qquad R(\tau,\xi)=\langle(\tau,\xi)\rangle, \qquad \|U\|_{(r,q)}^2=(2\pi)^{-(n+1)} \int R^{2r}h^{2q}|\widehat U(\tau,\xi)|^2\,d\tau\,d\xi. \tag{HC37} h(ξ)=⟨ξ⟩,R(τ,ξ)=⟨(τ,ξ)⟩,∥U∥(r,q)2​=(2π)−(n+1)∫R2rh2q∣U(τ,ξ)∣2dτdξ.(HC37)

The orders r,qr,qr,q are arbitrary real numbers. The argument also applies to a fixed finite-dimensional Hermitian coefficient space. The whole-space Hilbert structure, distributional multiplier domains and smooth-coefficient bounds are proved in the complete two-weight Hilbert and trace treatment, with H1–H3 coefficient multiplication, density and duality. A compactly supported smooth coefficient is a mixed symbol of order (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), so that theorem makes its multiplication bounded on every displayed scale. Localized smooth coefficients and their finitely many derivatives are sufficient below.

Let r+r^+r+ denote restriction to t>0t>0t>0. Define

H˙(r,q)={U∈H(r,q):supp⁡U⊂{t≥0}},H‾(r,q)=r+H(r,q),∥u∥H‾(r,q)=inf⁡r+U=u∥U∥(r,q).(HC38) \begin{aligned} \dot H^{(r,q)}&=\{U\in H^{(r,q)}:\operatorname{supp}U\subset\{t\ge0\}\},\\ \overline H^{(r,q)}&=r^+H^{(r,q)},\qquad \|u\|_{\overline H^{(r,q)}}=\inf_{r^+U=u}\|U\|_{(r,q)}. \end{aligned} \tag{HC38} H˙(r,q)H(r,q)​={U∈H(r,q):suppU⊂{t≥0}},=r+H(r,q),∥u∥H(r,q)​=r+U=uinf​∥U∥(r,q)​.​(HC38)

The dot space has the ambient norm. The bar space is the quotient by the closed subspace of distributions supported in t≤0t\le0t≤0. These subspaces are closed because norm convergence implies distributional convergence. Completeness of the quotient is the closed-subspace quotient theorem in the complete quotient and orthogonal projection proof, H1. An intrinsic normal derivative on the bar space is obtained by differentiating any extension and restricting; the derivative of a difference supported in t≤0t\le0t≤0 has the same support, so the definition is independent of the extension. It does not mean differentiating a zero extension.

Set

J+a=(h(Dx)+iDt)a,J−a=(h(Dx)−iDt)a,a∈R,(HC39) J_+^a=(h(D_x)+iD_t)^a,\qquad J_-^a=(h(D_x)-iD_t)^a,\qquad a\in\mathbb R, \tag{HC39} J+a​=(h(Dx​)+iDt​)a,J−a​=(h(Dx​)−iDt​)a,a∈R,(HC39)

Duality, embeddings and the supported decomposition

The full supported/restricted antidual proof is H3, which retains Proposition 10.2(b) with its density and orthogonal projection arguments. Apply it to h(Dx)qUh(D_x)^qUh(Dx​)qU and h(Dx)−qvh(D_x)^{-q}vh(Dx​)−qv. These maps preserve support and restriction and are isometries between the mixed and ordinary spaces; their factors cancel in the Fourier pairing. Consequently

(H˙(r,q))∗=H‾(−r,−q),(H‾(r,q))∗=H˙(−r,−q)(HC42) (\dot H^{(r,q)})^*=\overline H^{(-r,-q)},\qquad (\overline H^{(r,q)})^*=\dot H^{(-r,-q)} \tag{HC42} (H˙(r,q))∗=H(−r,−q),(H(r,q))∗=H˙(−r,−q)(HC42)

isometrically, with antiduals under the pairing linear in the first entry. Pair UUU with any whole-space extension VVV of the bar vector by (2π)−(n+1)∫U^V^‾(2\pi)^{-(n+1)}\int\widehat U\overline{\widehat V}(2π)−(n+1)∫UV. The programme duality proof shows independence of VVV and representation of every bounded functional. On smooth vectors it is the ordinary integral. A bar vector is not identified with an arbitrary supported extension.

The dense test space is also dense in the mixed dot space. Translate a dot vector forward by ϵ>0\epsilon>0ϵ>0; Fourier dominated convergence proves convergence in (HC37). A diagonal choice gives approximation by Cc∞(t>0)C_c^\infty(t>0)Cc∞​(t>0) in the dot space. Restrictions of whole-space smooth approximations are dense in the bar space. Boundary-supported distributions remain in the supported space at the negative orders where their ambient norm is finite.

Boundary operators survive changes of charts

The preceding trace is expressed in one collar. To use it at a curved initial surface, we must know which parts survive a change of collar. Here we use ordinary isotropic Sobolev spaces: H‾s=H‾(s,0)\overline H^s=\overline H^{(s,0)}Hs=H(s,0). We do not assert that an arbitrary boundary coordinate change preserves the two separate mixed orders.

A smooth manifold with boundary has Hausdorff, second-countable charts into relatively open subsets of t≥0t\ge0t≥0. Smooth chart transitions and their inverses extend smoothly to neighborhoods of the closed half-space. Near a boundary point, write a transition as Φ(x,t)=(F(x,t),tβ(x,t))\Phi(x,t)=(F(x,t),t\beta(x,t))Φ(x,t)=(F(x,t),tβ(x,t)). The integral identity

Φn(x,t)=t∫01∂tΦn(x,λt) dλ \Phi_n(x,t)=t\int_0^1\partial_t\Phi_n(x,\lambda t)\,d\lambda Φn​(x,t)=t∫01​∂t​Φn​(x,λt)dλ

gives this factorization. At the boundary the tangential derivative is invertible. The derivatives of the transition and its given inverse multiply to the identity, and the positive interior maps to the positive interior; hence β(x,0)>0\beta(x,0)>0β(x,0)>0. After shrinking, the extension has invertible derivative and β>0\beta>0β>0. The complete smooth inverse construction in the finite inverse theorem P3 in the exact U001 map supplies a neighborhood diffeomorphism. It preserves both normal sides.

Pullback by this diffeomorphism transports supported distributions to supported distributions. It also transports the full backward-supported kernel of interior restriction to that kernel. Thus it acts on restricted distributions independently of their extension. The supported action is independent of the chosen smooth extension of the chart transition as well. Two such extensions have identical derivatives of every order on the closed positive side. Their transformed tests therefore differ by a function flat there. A compactly localized distribution has finite order NNN. Cut a flat test off in a collar of width ε\varepsilonε; Taylor's formula to order greater than 2N2N2N makes its derivatives through order NNN tend uniformly to zero. The support condition discards the rest of the test. The finite-order bound then annihilates that difference. This proves independence even for distributions supported at the boundary.

The full localized all-real Sobolev coordinate proof is H1–H3 of the global boundary companion, using the complete Besov coordinate proof B2. Its integer estimates retain the Jacobian in the adjoint; the frequency-block proof gives every real intermediate order. Both sides are preserved, so the bound restricts to the dot space and descends to the bar quotient. The inverse bound gives equivalent norms, including finite-dimensional frame changes.

The actual locally finite coordinate cover and subordinate smooth partition are PS5. The same compact-shell construction works with half-balls: their relative interiors cover, their closed smaller half-balls are compact, and the usual coordinate bumps restrict smoothly. Dividing by the locally finite positive bump sum gives the boundary partition. Only finitely many terms meet a fixed compact set. These facts define the local supported and restricted spaces independently of charts and supply the finite patching below.

Use the refined factors and, for each branch, a scalar commuting test Φj\Phi_jΦj​, elliptic at the chosen initial covector, with its microsupport in an arbitrarily small transported cone. The boundary source is regular there. The exact tangential microsupport inclusion therefore makes Φjf\Phi_j fΦj​f smooth in a smaller compact collar; the same argument applies to ΦjRju\Phi_jR_juΦj​Rj​u and [Dt−Aj,Φj]Qju[D_t-A_j,\Phi_j]Q_ju[Dt​−Aj​,Φj​]Qj​u. All these terms belong to the dual conormal class before the smoothness upgrade. Thus

(Dt−Aj)(ΦjQju) (D_t-A_j)(\Phi_jQ_ju) (Dt​−Aj​)(Φj​Qj​u)

is smooth in that collar. The complete intrinsic trace action expresses (Qju)(0)(Q_ju)(0)(Qj​u)(0) as ∑k<mQjk(0)Dtku(0)\sum_{k<m}Q_{jk}(0)D_t^ku(0)∑k<m​Qjk​(0)Dtk​u(0). Proper tangential tests with the chosen microsupport make this initial value smooth, since all initial jets are regular at the selected covector.

The first-order smooth Cauchy solution agrees with ΦjQju\Phi_jQ_juΦj​Qj​u even if the latter was initially only a dual distribution. We prove the necessary distributional uniqueness, including the spatial test topology. Extend the scalar symbol smoothly to a short time interval on both sides of zero. Zero-extend the difference between the distribution and the smooth Cauchy solution for t≥0t\ge0t≥0. The intrinsic boundary-delta identity and its zero initial trace make the scalar equation homogeneous across zero. The distribution part has compact spatial output support; the smooth solution lies in every spatial Sobolev space. Their difference consequently acts continuously on smooth time-dependent spatial Schwartz tests on a compact temporal strip, with a finite number of seminorms.

For a compact smooth test forcing ggg, solve the backward adjoint first-order equation L∗z=gL^*z=gL∗z=g, with zero terminal value at TTT, using the first-order theorem at every Sobolev order. We verify that zzz is Schwartz in space without assuming distributional uniqueness to identify an unbounded moment. For integer N≥1N\ge1N≥1 take the bounded weights

wR(x)=⟨x⟩N(1+∣x∣2/R2)−N/2,R≥1.(HC26) w_R(x)=\langle x\rangle^N (1+|x|^2/R^2)^{-N/2},\qquad R\ge1. \tag{HC26} wR​(x)=⟨x⟩N(1+∣x∣2/R2)−N/2,R≥1.(HC26)

They tend locally smoothly to ⟨x⟩N\langle x\rangle^N⟨x⟩N. Their positive-order derivatives satisfy ∣∂xαwR∣≤CαN⟨x⟩N−∣α∣|\partial_x^\alpha w_R|\le C_{\alpha N}\langle x\rangle^{N-|\alpha|}∣∂xα​wR​∣≤CαN​⟨x⟩N−∣α∣, uniformly in RRR. For a bounded order-one symbol aaa, the normalized commutator

[a(x,Dx),wR]⟨x⟩1−N∈S0uniformly in R.(HC27) [a(x,D_x),w_R]\langle x\rangle^{1-N} \in S^0 \quad\text{uniformly in }R. \tag{HC27} [a(x,Dx​),wR​]⟨x⟩1−N∈S0uniformly in R.(HC27)

This is the usual ordinary product estimate with its zero-product term canceled. In the finite expansion every remaining term has a positive derivative of wRw_RwR​, a frequency derivative of aaa, and the indicated inverse weight, so its base derivatives are uniformly bounded and its frequency order is at most zero. In the integral remainder the ratio ⟨x+y⟩N−1/⟨x⟩N−1\langle x+y\rangle^{N-1}/\langle x\rangle^{N-1}⟨x+y⟩N−1/⟨x⟩N−1 has at most CN⟨y⟩N−1C_N\langle y\rangle^{N-1}CN​⟨y⟩N−1 growth. Integrate by parts in frequency more than N+n+2N+n+2N+n+2 times to absorb it and every fixed requested derivative. This gives the same uniform ordinary seminorm bounds for the actual remainder, rather than only a formal symbolic identity. The time derivatives of the symbol obey the identical estimate.

Assume all weights through N−1N-1N−1 of zzz have every spatial Sobolev order, uniformly on the finite strip. The equation for the legitimate bounded-weight function wRzw_RzwR​z has source wRg+[L∗,wR]zw_Rg+[L^*,w_R]zwR​g+[L∗,wR​]z. The first term is uniformly bounded in every Sobolev space because ggg is compact smooth; (HC27) and the inductive lower moment bound control the second uniformly in RRR. Its terminal value is zero. The ordinary first-order energy estimate therefore bounds wRzw_RzwR​z in every continuous spatial Sobolev norm uniformly in RRR. Here is the complete limit argument, using Fatou's inequality M3. The unweighted all-orders construction already makes z(t,⋅)z(t,\cdot)z(t,⋅) smooth. For each fixed time and each nonnegative integer kkk, all derivatives through kkk of wRzw_RzwR​z converge locally pointwise to those of ⟨x⟩Nz\langle x\rangle^Nz⟨x⟩Nz. Apply Fatou to the nonnegative finite sum of their squared moduli. The integer Sobolev norm is equivalent to this derivative sum by the Fourier binomial formula, so the uniform HkH^kHk energy bound gives an HkH^kHk bound for the limit, with a constant independent of time. Arbitrary real orders follow by embedding from larger integers. Distributional identification is the same local convergence. No subsequence or weak-compactness theorem is required. To obtain strong measurability, approximate this weighted vector by smooth spatial cutoffs: each cutoff is continuous into every spatial Sobolev space, and the cutoffs converge at each time in that space by the usual derivative-sum cutoff estimate. Their pointwise limit is strongly measurable. The commutator and equation then supply its Bochner primitive at one lower order; identification in distributions supplies the representative, and using one additional spatial order gives continuity at every desired order. The equation then gives its time continuity and time derivatives in every Sobolev order by the weak primitive argument, retaining only already controlled lower moments in the commutator. Induct on NNN, and use Sobolev embedding at arbitrarily large spatial order. We have proved every spatial Schwartz seminorm and every time derivative uniformly. No uniqueness assertion for an arbitrary tempered moment was used in this induction.

Choose ggg supported below some T0<TT_0<TT0​<T. The adjoint solution is zero on a neighborhood of TTT, by energy uniqueness and zero terminal data. Multiply zzz by a smooth time cutoff which is one from zero through T0T_0T0​, whose lower derivative support lies strictly in t<0t<0t<0, and whose upper derivative support lies in that zero terminal neighborhood. The lower commutator is disjoint from the zero-extended difference; the upper commutator is zero. The resulting compact-time Schwartz test is admissible for distributional adjoint pairing. It gives zero against ggg. Every compact smooth ggg on the shorter strip was arbitrary, so the difference is zero there. Thus every ΦjQju\Phi_jQ_juΦj​Qj​u is smooth up to the boundary.

It remains to recover uuu, rather than only its mmm quotients. Put

ek=m−1−k,zk=⟨Dx⟩ekDtku,Ajk=ΦjQjk⟨Dx⟩−ek.(HC21) e_k=m-1-k,\quad z_k=\langle D_x\rangle^{e_k}D_t^ku, \qquad A_{jk}=\Phi_jQ_{jk}\langle D_x\rangle^{-e_k}. \tag{HC21} ek​=m−1−k,zk​=⟨Dx​⟩ek​Dtk​u,Ajk​=Φj​Qjk​⟨Dx​⟩−ek​.(HC21)

This is an ordinary tangential order-zero matrix. Its principal matrix at the chosen covector has entries ϕj,0cjk/∣ξ∣ek\phi_{j,0}c_{jk}/|\xi|^{e_k}ϕj,0​cjk​/∣ξ∣ek​, where cjkc_{jk}cjk​ is the coefficient of τk\tau^kτk in qjq_jqj​. The polynomial interpolation identity proves that (cjk)(c_{jk})(cjk​) is invertible. Nonzero scalar row factors and column normalizations preserve invertibility; compactness and strict root separation give uniform inverse bounds on a smaller cone. The exact ordered ordinary matrix parametrix yields

CA=ΨI+K, C A=\Psi I+K, CA=ΨI+K,

where Ψ\PsiΨ is a tangential scalar test elliptic at the candidate and KKK is spatially smoothing on a smaller cone. Use one further conic cutoff to remove its off-cone microsupport. Interior propagation now traces singularities backward along each simple characteristic until forcing is encountered, the initial surface is reached, or the arc leaves the domain under consideration. If the backward segment stays in a compact part of the product domain until it reaches X0X_0X0​, every singularity arises from WF⁡(f)\operatorname{WF}(f)WF(f) on that segment or from the inverse image of the right-hand side of (HC20) under restriction of full covectors to the boundary. Locally in a small such collar this is the union of the mmm forward characteristic branches from those sources. A global assertion requires this backward-access condition, or boundary data at every other incoming part of the domain.

For example, on X=(−1,1)t×(0,1)xX=(-1,1)_t\times(0,1)_xX=(−1,1)t​×(0,1)x​, take ϕ=t\phi=tϕ=t, P=Dt−DxP=D_t-D_xP=Dt​−Dx​, and u=δ(x+t−3/2)u=\delta(x+t-3/2)u=δ(x+t−3/2) in X+X_+X+​. Testing v(0)=0v(0)=0v(0)=0 and arbitrary Dtv(0)D_tv(0)Dt​v(0) identifies u(0)u(0)u(0); then arbitrary v(0)v(0)v(0) identifies Dtu(0)D_tu(0)Dt​u(0) after that first cancellation.

Exercise 9 — intermediate: trace threshold. Compute the scaling of ∫Rτ2j(a2+τ2)−rdτ\int_\mathbb R\tau^{2j}(a^2+\tau^2)^{-r}d\tau∫R​τ2j(a2+τ2)−rdτ, for a>0a>0a>0, and find the exact convergence threshold. What is the trace Sobolev order after including a tangential weight a2qa^{2q}a2q?

Solution. Substitute τ=aσ\tau=a\sigmaτ=aσ. The integral is a2j+1−2r∫Rσ2j(1+σ2)−rdσa^{2j+1-2r}\int_\mathbb R\sigma^{2j}(1+\sigma^2)^{-r}d\sigmaa2j+1−2r∫R​σ2j(1+σ2)−rdσ. Its tail is integrable exactly when 2j−2r<−12j-2r<-12j−2r<−1, or r>j+1/2r>j+1/2r>j+1/2; equality diverges logarithmically. Cauchy–Schwarz in the normal Fourier variable therefore yields boundary order q+r−j−1/2q+r-j-1/2q+r−j−1/2. For integer r=mr=mr=m and j<mj<mj<m, the constant is Γ(j+1/2)Γ(m−j−1/2)/Γ(m)\Gamma(j+1/2)\Gamma(m-j-1/2)/\Gamma(m)Γ(j+1/2)Γ(m−j−1/2)/Γ(m). The endpoint is not part of the trace theorem.

Exact constant, with its proof. Define Γ(a)=∫0∞xa−1e−x dx\Gamma(a)=\int_0^\infty x^{a-1}e^{-x}\,dxΓ(a)=∫0∞​xa−1e−xdx for a>0a>0a>0. Near zero the power is integrable; the exponential bounds every power at infinity, so this is finite and positive, as in the included positive-order companion. For a,b>0a,b>0a,b>0, Tonelli M4 and the one-dimensional substitution v=uyv=uyv=uy, followed by w=u(1+y)w=u(1+y)w=u(1+y), give

Γ(a)Γ(b)=∫0∞ ⁣∫0∞ua−1vb−1e−u−v dv du=∫0∞yb−1(∫0∞ua+b−1e−u(1+y) du)dy=Γ(a+b)∫0∞yb−1(1+y)−a−b dy.(HC53) \begin{aligned} \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) &=\int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty u^{a-1}v^{b-1}e^{-u-v}\,dv\,du\\ &=\int_0^\infty y^{b-1} \left(\int_0^\infty u^{a+b-1}e^{-u(1+y)}\,du\right)dy\\ &=\Gamma(a+b)\int_0^\infty y^{b-1}(1+y)^{-a-b}\,dy . \end{aligned} \tag{HC53} Γ(a)Γ(b)​=∫0∞​∫0∞​ua−1vb−1e−u−vdvdu=∫0∞​yb−1(∫0∞​ua+b−1e−u(1+y)du)dy=Γ(a+b)∫0∞​yb−1(1+y)−a−bdy.​(HC53)

These substitutions can first be made on compact positive intervals, using the proved one-dimensional change of variables; monotone convergence then gives the displayed improper positive integrals. P3 M8 identifies those compact integrals with the measure integrals. All exchanges are nonnegative, so no unproved cancellation or analytic continuation enters. In the trace constant, split at zero and put y=σ2y=\sigma^2y=σ2. This gives ∫0∞yj−1/2(1+y)−r dy\int_0^\infty y^{j-1/2}(1+y)^{-r}\,dy∫0∞​yj−1/2(1+y)−rdy. Taking b=j+1/2b=j+1/2b=j+1/2 and a=r−j−1/2>0a=r-j-1/2>0a=r−j−1/2>0 proves

cr,j=Γ(j+1/2)Γ(r−j−1/2)Γ(r)(r>j+1/2).(HC54) c_{r,j}=\frac{\Gamma(j+1/2)\Gamma(r-j-1/2)}{\Gamma(r)} \quad (r>j+1/2). \tag{HC54} cr,j​=Γ(r)Γ(j+1/2)Γ(r−j−1/2)​(r>j+1/2).(HC54)

This proves the stated integer case and its full real-order extension.

Exercise 10 — intermediate: the mixed recovery inequalities. In (HC14), verify all B.2.9 inequalities and explain why the target normal order may exceed the original one.

Solution. The original pair is (m−1,r+q)(m-1,r+q)(m−1,r+q), the source pair in the theorem is (r+m,q)(r+m,q)(r+m,q), and the target is (r+m−1,q)(r+m-1,q)(r+m−1,q). Its normal order is at most r+mr+mr+m; its total order equals the original total r+q+m−1r+q+m-1r+q+m−1, and is one less than the source total r+q+mr+q+mr+q+m. These are exactly the three required inequalities. For r>0r>0r>0, the target normal order exceeds m−1m-1m−1. The equation supplies this gain; an additional requirement that the target normal order not exceed the original one would incorrectly exclude the intended application.

Exercise 11 — advanced: the negative-order correction. Prove every mixed order used in the correction after (HC15), including the normal-order distinction for [P,Dt][P,D_t][P,Dt​].

Solution. Differentiating the coefficients of P=∑PkDtkP=\sum P_kD_t^kP=∑Pk​Dtk​ gives [P,Dt]=i∑k<m(∂tPk)Dtk[P,D_t]=i\sum_{k<m}(\partial_tP_k)D_t^k[P,Dt​]=i∑k<m​(∂t​Pk​)Dtk​; the coefficient of DtmD_t^mDtm​ is constant and contributes zero. Each coefficient has spatial degree at most m−km-km−k. Applied to un∈H(r+m,q)u_n\in H^{(r+m,q)}un​∈H(r+m,q), the kkk-th term has normal order r+m−kr+m-kr+m−k and total order r+qr+qr+q. Embedding into (r+1,q−1)(r+1,q-1)(r+1,q−1) uses m−k≥1m-k\ge1m−k≥1 and equal total orders. The inductive correction belongs to (r+m,q−1)(r+m,q-1)(r+m,q−1), which embeds into (r+m−1,q)(r+m-1,q)(r+m−1,q), again with equal totals and one more original normal order. Both u0u_0u0​ and DtunD_tu_nDt​un​ lie in this last space; normal differentiation preserves closed half-space support, including its possible boundary distributions. Thus the final supported solution has exactly the requested order.

Exercise 12 — intermediate: support makes the uniqueness pairing legal. In the curved box, find a positive spatial margin for the joint support and explain every cutoff commutator in the adjoint pairing.

Solution. The joint support obeys ∣x∣≤ϵ2−δ<ϵ|x|\le\sqrt{\epsilon^2-\delta}<\epsilon∣x∣≤ϵ2−δ​<ϵ, so its spatial margin is ϵ−ϵ2−δ>0\epsilon-\sqrt{\epsilon^2-\delta}>0ϵ−ϵ2−δ​>0. Its lower time margin is at least ϵ2\epsilon^2ϵ2, and its upper time margin at least δ\deltaδ. It is compact in the open box. Choose η=1\eta=1η=1 on a neighborhood of this set and of the test forcing support. Every term of the differential commutator contains a positive derivative of η\etaη and a derivative of www, so its support lies where η\etaη varies and within supp⁡w\operatorname{supp}wsuppw. That set is disjoint from supp⁡u\operatorname{supp}usuppu. Consequently (u,[P∗,η]w)=0(u,[P^*,\eta]w)=0(u,[P∗,η]w)=0, while ηP∗w=g\eta P^*w=gηP∗w=g. This justifies the compact test identity used in uniqueness.

Exercise 13 — advanced: the correction sign in the smoothing factor. At a symbolic stage let RRR have leading symbol rrr and QQQ have polynomial q(τ)q(\tau)q(τ). Find the sign of the correction to AAA and give the quotient correction polynomial at leading order.

Solution. Replacing AAA by A+ℓA+\ellA+ℓ changes P−(Dt−A)QP-(D_t-A)QP−(Dt​−A)Q to R+ℓQR+\ell QR+ℓQ. Its value at the branch is r+ℓq(λ)r+\ell q(\lambda)r+ℓq(λ), so ℓ=−r/q(λ)\ell=-r/q(\lambda)ℓ=−r/q(λ). The quotient correction polynomial is (r+ℓq(τ))/(τ−λ)(r+\ell q(\tau))/(\tau-\lambda)(r+ℓq(τ))/(τ−λ), of degree at most m−2m-2m−2, because the numerator vanishes at λ\lambdaλ. It is added to QQQ, rather than subtracted: the new defect is R+ℓQ−(Dt−A−ℓ)SR+\ell Q-(D_t-A-\ell)SR+ℓQ−(Dt​−A−ℓ)S. At operator level (HC17) retains coefficient derivatives and ordinary composition, and the residual drops one spatial order. For m=1m=1m=1, q=1q=1q=1, the numerator is zero and there is no quotient polynomial.

Exercise 14 — advanced: normalize every quotient column. For the cubic in Exercise 1, form the order-zero quotient matrix on ξ>0\xi>0ξ>0, using z=(∣ξ∣2u,∣ξ∣Dtu,Dt2u)z=(|\xi|^2u,|\xi|D_tu,D_t^2u)z=(∣ξ∣2u,∣ξ∣Dt​u,Dt2​u). Find its inverse and recover all three jets.

Solution. With unit commuting principal row factors the matrix is

A=(0−21−401021),A−1=(1/8−1/41/8−1/401/41/201/2). A=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2&1\\-4&0&1\\0&2&1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/8&-1/4&1/8\\-1/4&0&1/4\\1/2&0&1/2\end{pmatrix}. A=​0−40​−202​111​​,A−1=​1/8−1/41/2​−1/400​1/81/41/2​​.

For wj=qj(Dt)uw_j=q_j(D_t)uwj​=qj​(Dt​)u, the reconstruction is z0=(w1−2w2+w3)/8z_0=(w_1-2w_2+w_3)/8z0​=(w1​−2w2​+w3​)/8, z1=(−w1+w3)/4z_1=(-w_1+w_3)/4z1​=(−w1​+w3​)/4, and z2=(w1+w3)/2z_2=(w_1+w_3)/2z2​=(w1​+w3​)/2. Divide the first by ∣ξ∣2|\xi|^2∣ξ∣2 and the second by ∣ξ∣|\xi|∣ξ∣ to recover u,Dtuu,D_tuu,Dt​u. This is the full system; retaining only one quotient would not recover arbitrary jets. In variable coefficients these matrix products acquire lower-order symbolic corrections, handled by the ordinary ordered parametrix and its residuals.

Exercise 15 — intermediate: Hamiltonian parameter versus forward time. Compute HpH_pHp​ on the two branches of p=τ2−c2ξ2p=\tau^2-c^2\xi^2p=τ2−c2ξ2 and compare with Hτ∓cξH_{\tau\mp c\xi}Hτ∓cξ​. Which parameter should define forward Cauchy propagation?

Solution. On τ=cξ\tau=c\xiτ=cξ, p=(τ−cξ)(τ+cξ)p=(\tau-c\xi)(\tau+c\xi)p=(τ−cξ)(τ+cξ), so Hp=2cξHτ−cξH_p=2c\xi H_{\tau-c\xi}Hp​=2cξHτ−cξ​; on τ=−cξ\tau=-c\xiτ=−cξ, Hp=−2cξHτ+cξH_p=-2c\xi H_{\tau+c\xi}Hp​=−2cξHτ+cξ​. The spatial velocities of the normalized branch fields are −c-c−c and ccc, respectively, and both have t˙=1\dot t=1t˙=1. The sign of 2cξ2c\xi2cξ, or of −2cξ-2c\xi−2cξ, can reverse the parameter of HpH_pHp​. Forward Cauchy propagation uses increasing ttt, equivalently the normalized first-order branch parameter, while the unparameterized characteristic curves are the same.

Exercise 16 — intermediate: a raw boundary derivative is different. Let uuu be smooth on t≥0t\ge0t≥0, with nonzero initial value. Compute the derivative of its zero extension and the intrinsic normal derivative. Why can an arbitrary ambient derivative not supply the Cauchy jet used in (HC20)?

Solution. Since DtH=−iδD_tH=-i\deltaDt​H=−iδ, Dt(Hu)=H(Dtu)−iu(0)δD_t(Hu)=H(D_tu)-iu(0)\deltaDt​(Hu)=H(Dt​u)−iu(0)δ. Adding iu(0)δiu(0)\deltaiu(0)δ gives the supported representative of the intrinsic derivative. The raw ambient derivative includes a distribution concentrated on the boundary, even though the interior derivative is smooth. An arbitrary extension can add further boundary-supported distributions without changing its interior restriction. The canonical dual conormal extension and its intrinsic trace remove this ambiguity; (HC20) uses those traces and all mmm normal jets.

Exercise 17 — advanced: why tangential smoothing alone is insufficient. Let BBB have a smooth spatial kernel K(x,y)K(x,y)K(x,y), and take u(t,x)=δ(t−t∗)g(x)u(t,x)=\delta(t-t_*)g(x)u(t,x)=δ(t−t∗​)g(x), with compact smooth ggg and Bg≠0Bg\ne0Bg=0. Compare this with its action in the boundary proof.

Solution. Bu=δ(t−t∗)Bg(x)Bu=\delta(t-t_*)Bg(x)Bu=δ(t−t∗​)Bg(x) still has pure temporal wavefront at every point where Bg≠0Bg\ne0Bg=0; no spatial-frequency decay removes the normal delta. In the interior propagation proof the ordinary cutoff first excludes all pure temporal wavefront directions of the compact input. In the boundary proof, the input is in N\mathcal NN, and the exact tangential theorem first removes every compressed boundary covector for a spatially smoothing output. Closedness on a compact output collar then excludes interior wavefront approaching the boundary; the conormal/dual intersection upgrades it to full smoothness. These are the actual extra hypotheses and mechanisms.

Exercise 18 — advanced: an incoming spatial edge. Verify the domain example at the end of Section 9, including extendibility, the equation, the initial traces and the characteristic through (t,x)=(3/4,3/4)(t,x)=(3/4,3/4)(t,x)=(3/4,3/4). State the valid propagation conclusion.

Solution. The ambient distribution δ(x+t−3/2)\delta(x+t-3/2)δ(x+t−3/2) restricts to the interior solution, so it is extendible. Its two partial derivatives are both δ′(x+t−3/2)\delta'(x+t-3/2)δ′(x+t−3/2), hence (Dt−Dx)u=0(D_t-D_x)u=0(Dt​−Dx​)u=0. At any (0,x0)(0,x_0)(0,x0​) with 0<x0<10<x_0<10<x0​<1, a sufficiently small neighborhood has x+t<3/2x+t<3/2x+t<3/2, so uuu and every initial jet vanish there. Its ordinary wavefront along the graph consists of nonzero covectors a(dt+dx)a(dt+dx)a(dt+dx), which satisfy τ−ξ=0\tau-\xi=0τ−ξ=0. The normalized branch has t˙=1,x˙=−1\dot t=1,\dot x=-1t˙=1,x˙=−1, so its backward line from (3/4,3/4)(3/4,3/4)(3/4,3/4) reaches (1/2,1)(1/2,1)(1/2,1) and exits the open spatial interval, before reaching t=0t=0t=0. The boundary equality at X0X_0X0​ is valid, and local propagation follows this incoming characteristic. To deduce a global containment from initial data and forcing alone, require backward characteristics to remain in the domain until they reach the initial surface, or supply data on the incoming spatial edge.

Exercise 19 — advanced: interior distributions need not be extendible. On t>0t>0t>0, let u(t,x)=e1/tg(x)u(t,x)=e^{1/t}g(x)u(t,x)=e1/tg(x), where ggg is a nonnegative nonzero smooth function of compact support. Show that uuu is an interior distribution and that no distribution across t=0t=0t=0 restricts to it. Explain which hypothesis of the boundary theorem this example tests.

Solution. The function is smooth on the open half-space, so it defines a distribution there. Choose a nonnegative spatial test ψ\psiψ with c0=∫gψ>0c_0=\int g\psi>0c0​=∫gψ>0, and a nonnegative normal test η∈Cc∞((1,2))\eta\in C_c^\infty((1,2))η∈Cc∞​((1,2)) with integral one. For ηϵ(t)=ϵ−1η(t/ϵ)\eta_\epsilon(t)=\epsilon^{-1}\eta(t/\epsilon)ηϵ​(t)=ϵ−1η(t/ϵ), all these product tests are supported in one fixed compact neighborhood of t=0t=0t=0, and

(u,ηϵψ)≥c0e1/(2ϵ).(HC32) (u,\eta_\epsilon\psi)\ge c_0 e^{1/(2\epsilon)}. \tag{HC32} (u,ηϵ​ψ)≥c0​e1/(2ϵ).(HC32)

If an extension UUU existed, its continuity on tests supported in that compact set would give an order MMM and ∣(U,ηϵψ)∣≤Cϵ−M−1|(U,\eta_\epsilon\psi)|\le C\epsilon^{-M-1}∣(U,ηϵ​ψ)∣≤Cϵ−M−1. Restriction identifies this pairing with the preceding one, since its support lies in t>0t>0t>0. Exponential growth exceeds that polynomial for small ϵ\epsilonϵ, a contradiction. Thus membership in D′(X+)\mathcal D'(X_+)D′(X+​) alone does not give the extendibility required for D′‾(X+)\overline{\mathcal D'}(X_+)D′(X+​), much less the canonical N\mathcal NN extension and intrinsic jets. This example tests the distribution class; it is not asserted to solve an equation with the forcing hypotheses of the boundary theorem.

Exercise 20 — intermediate: forcing contributes boundary wavefront. Take P=DtP=D_tP=Dt​, f(t,x)=δ(x)f(t,x)=\delta(x)f(t,x)=δ(x), and zero initial value. Compute an extendible solution and its compressed boundary wavefront. Explain why the forcing term is necessary in (HC20).

Solution. The monic first-order symbol is p=τp=\taup=τ, with pτ=1p_\tau=1pτ​=1, so the strict condition holds. The solution u=itδ(x)u=it\delta(x)u=itδ(x) satisfies Dtu=δ(x)D_tu=\delta(x)Dt​u=δ(x) and u(0)=0u(0)=0u(0)=0. These distributions are smooth in time with values in spatial distributions, extend across the boundary, and have no ordinary wavefront in pure temporal directions. Their canonical extensions and intrinsic jets belong to N\mathcal NN. The only possible compressed singularities lie at t=0,x=0,ζ=0,ξ≠0t=0,x=0,\zeta=0,\xi\ne0t=0,x=0,ζ=0,ξ=0, by tangential localization away from the wavefront of δ(x)\delta(x)δ(x). Every one is present: the intrinsic derivative is fff, its initial trace is δ(x)\delta(x)δ(x), and the differential forward inclusion (HC25) followed by the exact trace inclusion gives

{(0,0;ξ,0):ξ≠0}=WF⁡(δ)⊂WF⁡b(f)⊂WF⁡b(u).(HC33) \{(0,0;\xi,0):\xi\ne0\} =\operatorname{WF}(\delta)\subset\operatorname{WF}_b(f) \subset\operatorname{WF}_b(u). \tag{HC33} {(0,0;ξ,0):ξ=0}=WF(δ)⊂WFb​(f)⊂WFb​(u).(HC33)

The first inclusion regards the ordinary trace covector as the corresponding boundary covector. The opposite containment was just localized directly, so this describes the boundary wavefront exactly. All initial data in the order-one problem vanish, yet the boundary forcing has nonempty wavefront. Including WF⁡b(f)\operatorname{WF}_b(f)WFb​(f) in the boundary equality is essential.

Exercise 21 — intermediate: the minimal extension of an exponential. In the one-dimensional normal model let uα(t)=e−αtu_\alpha(t)=e^{-\alpha t}uα​(t)=e−αt on t>0t>0t>0, with α>0\alpha>0α>0. Compute its minimal H1H^1H1 extension from (HC41), its squared quotient norm and the ratio of the two lower squared norms in (HC45) to that quotient norm. Determine when the lower bound is attained.

Solution. Here J−=1−∂tJ_-=1-\partial_tJ−​=1−∂t​, so g=(1+α)e−αtg=(1+\alpha)e^{-\alpha t}g=(1+α)e−αt. The inverse has kernel etH(−t)e^tH(-t)etH(−t), since (1−∂t)(etH(−t))=δ0(1-\partial_t)(e^tH(-t))=\delta_0(1−∂t​)(etH(−t))=δ0​. Thus

E1uα(t)=et∫max⁡(t,0)∞(1+α)e−(1+α)s ds={e−αt,t≥0,et,t<0.(HC49) E_1u_\alpha(t)=e^t\int_{\max(t,0)}^\infty(1+\alpha)e^{-(1+\alpha)s}\,ds =\begin{cases}e^{-\alpha t},&t\ge0,\\ e^t,&t<0.\end{cases} \tag{HC49} E1​uα​(t)=et∫max(t,0)∞​(1+α)e−(1+α)sds={e−αt,et,​t≥0,t<0.​(HC49)

The boundary values agree, so its weak first derivative has no delta. The squared H1H^1H1 norm is (1+α2)/(2α)+1=(1+α)2/(2α)=∥g∥22(1+\alpha^2)/(2\alpha)+1=(1+\alpha)^2/(2\alpha)=\|g\|_2^2(1+α2)/(2α)+1=(1+α)2/(2α)=∥g∥22​, which is minimal by (HC41). The two lower squared quotient norms sum to (1+α2)/(2α)(1+\alpha^2)/(2\alpha)(1+α2)/(2α). Their ratio is (1+α2)/(1+α)2(1+\alpha^2)/(1+\alpha)^2(1+α2)/(1+α)2, at least 1/21/21/2 because (α−1)2≥0(\alpha-1)^2\ge0(α−1)2≥0, with equality exactly at α=1\alpha=1α=1. On a mixed collar the same operator E1E_1E1​ commutes with every tangential Sobolev weight, including nonintegral orders; it selects one extension for their intersections. This normal model exhibits its boundary mechanism, not a nonzero constant vector in a spatial L2L^2L2 space.

Exercise 22 — advanced: a supported delta and the sign of the decomposition. In one normal dimension determine the orders rrr for which δ0∈Hr(R)\delta_0\in H^r(\mathbb R)δ0​∈Hr(R). Apply (HC44) to it. Verify the component orders, support and equality as ambient distributions, including the boundary term.

Solution. Since δ^0=1\widehat\delta_0=1δ0​=1, its squared norm is (2π)−1∫(1+τ2)r dτ(2\pi)^{-1}\int(1+\tau^2)^r\,d\tau(2π)−1∫(1+τ2)rdτ, finite exactly for r<−1/2r<-1/2r<−1/2. The inverse of J+=1+∂tJ_+=1+\partial_tJ+​=1+∂t​ has kernel H(t)e−tH(t)e^{-t}H(t)e−t. Therefore

f0=H(t)e−t,fn=iH(t)e−t,Dtfn=δ0−H(t)e−t,f0+Dtfn=δ0.(HC50) f_0=H(t)e^{-t},\qquad f_n=iH(t)e^{-t},\qquad D_tf_n=\delta_0-H(t)e^{-t},\qquad f_0+D_tf_n=\delta_0. \tag{HC50} f0​=H(t)e−t,fn​=iH(t)e−t,Dt​fn​=δ0​−H(t)e−t,f0​+Dt​fn​=δ0​.(HC50)

Both components have forward support. The Fourier modulus of H(t)e−tH(t)e^{-t}H(t)e−t is (1+τ2)−1/2(1+\tau^2)^{-1/2}(1+τ2)−1/2, so each squared Hr+1H^{r+1}Hr+1 norm equals the displayed squared HrH^rHr norm of δ0\delta_0δ0​. In this zero-dimensional tangential model the extra tangential weight is one. The ambient derivative must retain its delta; deleting it would give zero instead of the supported source. On restriction to t>0t>0t>0, the same source is zero, which explains why the bar and dot problems differ at the boundary.

Exercise 23 — advanced: two order-three boundary operators. In a two-dimensional collar, compare B1u=(Dx2Dtu)∣t=0B_1u=(D_x^2D_tu)|_{t=0}B1​u=(Dx2​Dt​u)∣t=0​ and B2u=(Dt3u)∣t=0B_2u=(D_t^3u)|_{t=0}B2​u=(Dt3​u)∣t=0​. Find their total and transversal orders and their guaranteed maps on restricted HsH^sHs. Under X=x+ct,T=atX=x+ct,T=atX=x+ct,T=at, with a>0a>0a>0, compute B1B_1B1​ in the new chart. Show explicitly why B2B_2B2​ has no continuous extension from restricted H2H^2H2 to H−3/2H^{-3/2}H−3/2, although B1B_1B1​ does.

Solution. Both total orders are three. Their transversal orders are one and three, respectively. Formula (HC51) gives target Hs−7/2H^{s-7/2}Hs−7/2 for B1B_1B1​ when s>3/2s>3/2s>3/2, and for B2B_2B2​ when s>7/2s>7/2s>7/2. If v(X,T)=u(X−cT/a,T/a)v(X,T)=u(X-cT/a,T/a)v(X,T)=u(X−cT/a,T/a), the actual chain rule gives Dx=DXD_x=D_XDx​=DX​ and Dt=cDX+aDTD_t=cD_X+aD_TDt​=cDX​+aDT​. Therefore

B1u=(cDX3v+aDX2DTv)∣T=0.(HC52) B_1u=\bigl(cD_X^3v+aD_X^2D_Tv\bigr)|_{T=0}. \tag{HC52} B1​u=(cDX3​v+aDX2​DT​v)∣T=0​.(HC52)

The added term has transversal order zero; the nonzero coefficient aaa retains transversal order one. The change of collar does not raise that order to three.

Every member is smooth up to the boundary, so a continuous extension agreeing with the smooth boundary operator would contradict this sequence. Total order alone cannot select the trace threshold.

Source and prerequisite notes

The historical source for the higher-order statements is Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators III, approved 2007 eBook, ISBN 978-3-540-49938-1, Section 23.2, printed pages 390–400 (PDF pages 405–415). The progression above includes Lemma 23.2.1, Theorem 23.2.2, Definition 23.2.3, Theorem 23.2.4, Propositions 23.2.5–23.2.6, Theorem 23.2.7, Lemma 23.2.8 and Theorems 23.2.9–23.2.10. The global forward reading of the last consequence is qualified by the domain-access condition and the explicit incoming-edge example, as required by local propagation.

Appendix B.2, especially B.2.1, B.2.3–B.2.4, B.2.6–B.2.7 and B.2.9–B.2.10, supplies the mathematical antecedents for the mixed spaces. The actual programme proofs are the included MH two-weight and support/duality companions, GB coordinate bounds and the complete Section 4 above. The ordinary/tangential composition antecedent is III, Theorem 18.1.35; the exact all-remainder proof is the FC spacetime companion. Noncharacteristic pullback uses I, Theorem 8.2.4, approved 2003 eBook ISBN 978-3-642-61497-2; the included complete pullback and slice companion proves the needed statements and retains its GFDL notices.

Boundary extension and jets use NE's full weighted normal equation, CNF's dual action and intrinsic jets, BW's complete compressed differential proof, normal and tangential action and smooth testers and exact trace consequences. These retain the existing AN-03 bridge material by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), with Codex editorial contributions, and its source context in Hörmander III, 18.3.31–18.3.33. The actual ordered quotient inverse uses the included ordinary matrix parametrix. The positive-real beta bridge was compared with AN03-U008 Section 16.9; (HC53) gives an independent positive-integral proof using only the exact earlier measure and one-dimensional substitution proofs.

The current owner review covers the complete written arguments and all twenty-three original solutions. The current proof map records each exact provider; finite model checks supplement the proofs. Independent human review, the remaining course and public clearance are separate and remain pending.
